title: Lipophilicity: LogP & LogD
summary: The single property that touches nearly every part of a drug's fate.

lessons.title: Partition coefficients: logP

levels.kid:
Imagine a glass with oil floating on top of water. Now drop in a tiny bit of a medicine and shake it.

Some medicines like the oil better. Some like the water better. Chemists count how much ends up in each layer.

That number is called **logP**. A big logP means the molecule loves oil (we say it is **greasy**). A small or negative logP means it loves water.

Why care? Your body is both! Blood is watery, but the walls of your cells are oily. A good medicine has to like water enough to travel in blood, and like oil enough to slip through cell walls. Not too greasy, not too watery. Just right, like Goldilocks.
levels.hs:
**Lipophilicity** means "fat-loving": how much a molecule prefers an oily environment over water. It is measured with the **partition coefficient, P**.

To measure it, chemists shake a compound with two liquids that do not mix: **1-octanol** (an oily alcohol) and water. Then they measure the concentration in each layer:

- P = [compound in octanol] / [compound in water]
- logP = log10 of P

Because it is a log scale, logP = 2 means 100 times more in octanol than in water. logP = 0 means equal amounts. logP = -1 means 10 times more in water.

Some real values: methanol is about -0.8, ethanol about -0.3, phenol about 1.5, benzene about 2.1 and toluene about 2.7. Notice the pattern: adding carbon makes things greasier, and adding OH groups makes things more water-loving.

Why octanol? It has a long greasy chain plus one OH group that can hydrogen-bond, a bit like the fatty but polar membranes of cells. It is not a perfect copy of a membrane, but it predicts a lot.

Most oral drugs have logP between about 0 and 5. Too low and the drug cannot cross membranes; too high and it will not dissolve.
levels.college:
**Definition.** P is the ratio of equilibrium concentrations of the **neutral** species between 1-octanol and water: logP = log10([X]oct/[X]aq). Strictly, both phases are mutually saturated: water-saturated octanol contains a substantial amount of water (roughly a quarter of its molecules), which is part of why it mimics a hydrated membrane interface.

**Thermodynamics.** logP reports the free energy of transfer from water to octanol: ΔG(transfer) = -2.303RT·logP, so one logP unit is about 1.4 kcal/mol at 25 °C. The driving force is largely the **hydrophobic effect**: water must organize around nonpolar surface, and moving that surface into octanol releases water, which is favourable mostly for entropic reasons near room temperature.

**Additivity.** Hansch and Fujita showed that substituent effects are roughly additive. The aromatic **π constant** is π(X) = logP(Ph-X) - logP(Ph-H). Approximate values: Cl +0.71, Br +0.86, CH3 +0.56, CF3 +0.88, F +0.14, OCH3 -0.02, OH -0.67, NH2 -1.23. Each extra CH2 adds roughly 0.5. So chlorobenzene (about 2.84) is benzene (2.13) plus π(Cl).

**Molecular contributors.** Size and nonpolar surface raise logP. Hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors lower it, donors especially, because water solvates them well and octanol only partly. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can hide polarity and raise logP above additive predictions.

**Why it matters.** Lipophilicity correlates with membrane permeability, plasma protein binding, volume of distribution, metabolic clearance, solubility (inversely), off-target binding and potency itself. That is why it is often called the most important single physicochemical property in drug design.
levels.phd:
**Solvent-system dependence.** The Collander relationship links partition coefficients across solvent pairs: logP(solvent 2) = a·logP(octanol) + b. It holds only within families of similar hydrogen-bonding character. Octanol is an amphiprotic solvent that accepts and donates hydrogen bonds; alkanes (hexadecane, cyclohexane) do neither. The difference **ΔlogP = logP(oct) - logP(alkane)** therefore isolates a molecule's hydrogen-bonding capacity, especially donor strength, which explains why alkane-based systems sometimes track blood-brain barrier penetration better than octanol.

**Solvation equations.** Abraham's linear free-energy relationship decomposes logP as c + eE + sS + aA + bB + vV, where A and B are overall hydrogen-bond acidity and basicity, S dipolarity/polarizability, E excess molar refraction and V McGowan volume. For octanol/water, the volume term is large and positive and the basicity term is strongly negative; the acidity term is near zero, because octanol accepts hydrogen bonds almost as well as water does. That is why donors cost much more in alkane systems than in octanol.

**Is octanol a membrane?** No. Bilayers are anisotropic: a charged headgroup region, an ordered interfacial zone and a disordered core. Partitioning into bilayers depends on shape and orientation, and charged amphiphiles can partition into membranes far more than octanol logD predicts. Octanol works because it captures the dominant volume-versus-hydrogen-bonding trade-off, not because it is structurally membrane-like.

**Non-additivity.** Proximity effects (two polar groups that are close interact and do not cost twice), intramolecular hydrogen bonds, conformational folding that buries polar surface, and electronic effects in aromatic systems all break simple fragment sums. These deviations are where calculated values fail most, and where clever design finds extra permeability.
levels.expert:
In a project, logP is a property you manage on every compound, not a number you look up once.

**How senior chemists use it.**
- Track lipophilicity alongside potency from the first hit. Potency gained by adding grease is the easiest gain and often the most expensive later.
- Remember the π shortcuts when making design decisions at the whiteboard: a chlorine adds about 0.7, a methyl about 0.5, swapping a phenyl for a pyridine usually removes roughly 1 to 1.5, and a hydroxyl subtracts about 0.7 on an aromatic ring (more on an aliphatic chain).
- For ionizable compounds, logP alone misleads; logD at the relevant pH is what the biology sees (next lesson).

**Common pitfalls.**
- Treating a calculated value as measured. Different programs can disagree by more than a log unit for unusual scaffolds.
- Ignoring that logP is a property of the neutral form. A strongly basic amine with a high logP may be quite polar at pH 7.4.
- Over-trusting additivity when polar groups sit next to each other or can form intramolecular hydrogen bonds.

**Clinical connection.** Lipophilicity shapes where drugs go in patients. Highly lipophilic anaesthetic agents act fast on the brain and then redistribute into fat; this is part of why a single bolus of a lipophilic induction agent wears off quickly. Lipophilic beta-blockers such as propranolol enter the CNS more than hydrophilic atenolol, which is one reason CNS side effects like vivid dreams differ between them. In neurosurgical and ICU practice, prolonged infusions of lipophilic sedatives accumulate in fat and wake-up times stretch out, a pharmacokinetic consequence of a physicochemical property set at the bench.

keyPoints: logP = log10 of the octanol/water concentration ratio of the neutral compound.
Each logP unit = 10-fold preference; one unit is about 1.4 kcal/mol of transfer free energy.
Hansch π constants: Cl about +0.7, CH3 about +0.5, OH about -0.7 on an aromatic ring.
Hydrogen-bond donors and polar groups lower logP; carbon and halogens raise it.
Most oral drugs sit roughly between logP 0 and 5.

examples.tr: Adding Cl raises logP by about 0.7 (the π value of Cl).
More lipophilic propranolol enters the brain more; hydrophilic atenolol much less.

advancedTest.q: Two polar groups placed next to each other often make a molecule MORE lipophilic than fragment addition predicts because:

advancedTest.explain: Proximity and intramolecular hydrogen bonds reduce the exposed polarity, a classic cause of non-additivity.

lessons.title: LogD and pH dependence

levels.kid:
Some medicines can wear a tiny electric **charge**, like a little plus or minus sticker.

A molecule with a charge loves water and hates oil. A molecule with no charge can sneak into oil.

Whether a molecule wears its sticker depends on how sour or not sour the place is. Your stomach is very sour (acid). Your blood is just a tiny bit not-sour.

So the same medicine can be greasy in one part of your body and watery in another! Chemists use a number called **logD** to say how greasy a medicine really is at one exact place, like in blood. It is logP, but it remembers the charge.
levels.hs:
Many drugs are **acids** or **bases**, so they can gain or lose a proton (H+) and become charged. A charged molecule (an ion) is very well solvated by water and hardly enters octanol or membranes.

The **pKa** tells you the pH where half the molecules are charged.
- An acid (like a carboxylic acid, pKa about 4 to 5) is mostly **charged at pH above its pKa**.
- A base (like an amine, pKa about 9 to 10) is mostly **charged at pH below its pKa**.

**logD** (distribution coefficient) is the octanol/water ratio of ALL forms of the compound, charged and neutral, at a stated pH. Chemists most often report **logD7.4**, the pH of blood.

Rule of thumb: each pH unit beyond the pKa (on the ionizing side) lowers logD by about one unit, because ten times more of the drug is charged.

Example: an amine with pKa 9.4 and logP 3. At pH 7.4 it is about 100 times more charged than neutral, so its logD7.4 is about 1. For a neutral molecule with nothing to ionize, logD = logP at every pH.

This is why a drug can be absorbed well in one part of the gut and poorly in another.
levels.college:
**Equations.** Assuming only the neutral species partitions:
- Monoprotic acid: logD = logP - log10(1 + 10^(pH - pKa))
- Monoprotic base: logD = logP - log10(1 + 10^(pKa - pH))

Far from the pKa this reduces to a slope of one log unit per pH unit; at pH = pKa, logD = logP - 0.30.

**Worked example.** Ibuprofen: pKa about 4.5, logP about 4. At pH 7.4 the term is log10(1 + 10^2.9), about 2.9, so logD7.4 is about 1.1. In the stomach (pH 2) it is essentially neutral and logD is about 4.

**Ion-pair partitioning.** Ions do partition into octanol, as ion pairs with counter-ions, typically 3 to 4 log units below the neutral form. So logD does not fall forever: it flattens out at extreme pH. Counter-ion identity and ionic strength matter.

**Zwitterions and ampholytes** (an acid plus a base, as in cetirizine) show bell-shaped or flat logD profiles, often low across the physiological range.

**Physiological pH map.**
- Stomach: about 1.5 to 3.5 (fasted)
- Small intestine: about 6 to 7.5
- Blood and most tissue: 7.4
- Lysosomes: about 4.5 to 5
- Inflamed or ischaemic tissue: lower than normal

**pH-partition hypothesis.** Neutral species cross membranes; ions largely do not. At equilibrium, a weak base concentrates in the more acidic compartment, because it gets protonated and trapped there. This is ion trapping.

**Consequences.** logD7.4, not logP, correlates best with plasma protein binding, permeability at intestinal pH ranges, hERG risk and metabolic clearance for ionizable drugs.
levels.phd:
**Beyond the simple model.** The textbook equations ignore ion partitioning, self-association and the membrane's own electrostatics. Real bilayers carry negatively charged phospholipids (phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylinositol) and a dipole potential. Protonated amphiphilic amines insert into bilayers with their charged nitrogen at the headgroup and their lipophilic tail in the core; liposome/water partitioning of cationic amphiphiles can be orders of magnitude higher than octanol logD predicts. Acids, by contrast, are repelled by anionic headgroups.

**Microscopic vs macroscopic pKa.** For polyprotic or zwitterionic molecules, several microspecies coexist (for example, neutral vs zwitterionic tautomers of an amino acid). Their relative populations, not just the macroscopic pKa values, determine logD. Zwitterion formation can mask lipophilicity and even support CNS penetration in rare cases, but usually lowers passive permeability.

**The acid microclimate.** The unstirred water layer at the intestinal surface is slightly more acidic than bulk lumen. The pH at the membrane, not the bulk, governs ionization there, which is part of why weak acids are absorbed better than naive calculations suggest, alongside the huge small-intestinal surface area.

**Lysosomal trapping.** Lipophilic weak bases (pKa above about 8, logP above about 2) diffuse into lysosomes, become protonated at pH about 5 and accumulate. The trapped amount can be very large, raising tissue binding and volume of distribution, and contributing to **drug-induced phospholipidosis**: cationic amphiphilic drugs complex with phospholipids and inhibit lysosomal phospholipases, producing lamellar bodies. Amiodarone and chloroquine are classic examples.

**Tumour pH.** Many solid tumours have an acidic extracellular space but near-neutral intracellular pH, which tends to exclude weak bases from cells and favour weak acids. pH also drives chemistry, not just partitioning: the brain-tumour drug temozolomide is stable in acidic stomach fluid but opens spontaneously at physiological pH to its active methylating species, so pH acts as its activation switch.
levels.expert:
**Practical use.** Always know where every ionizable centre is and its approximate pKa before trusting any lipophilicity number. A base with pKa 10 and an acid with pKa 4 are both more than 99% ionized at 7.4.

**Tuning pKa is one of the most powerful levers in optimization.**
- Lowering an amine's pKa from 10 to about 8 (by adding a nearby fluorine, an adjacent ether oxygen, or switching piperidine to morpholine) raises logD7.4 without adding grease, often improving permeability and reducing hERG blockade by changing the cation's behaviour.
- Adding a carboxylic acid usually crushes logD7.4, cuts brain penetration, lowers volume of distribution and increases albumin binding. This is how second-generation antihistamines like cetirizine (an ampholyte) reduced sedation compared with their parent drugs.

**Pitfalls.**
- Reporting logD at one pH and assuming it describes absorption: the drug sees pH from about 2 to 7.5 on its way through the gut.
- Forgetting that measured logD of strong bases at 7.4 may be dominated by ion-pair partitioning, not by the neutral form.
- Mixing logP and logD across a series where some compounds are ionizable and some are not, which creates false trends.

**Clinical echoes.**
- Urine alkalinization increases ionization of weak acids such as salicylate in the tubule, trapping them in urine and speeding elimination; this is a recognized part of salicylate poisoning management.
- Local anaesthetics (weak bases) work poorly in infected, acidic tissue because more drug is protonated and cannot cross the nerve membrane.
- Ion trapping explains why weak bases accumulate in acidic compartments, from lysosomes to breast milk, which is relevant to drug safety discussions in lactation.

keyPoints: logD = octanol/water ratio of ALL species at a given pH; logP is neutral form only.
For a neutral compound, logD = logP at any pH.
Each pH unit past the pKa (on the ionizing side) lowers logD by about 1 unit.
Acids are charged above their pKa; bases are charged below it.
Lipophilic weak bases get trapped in acidic compartments such as lysosomes.

examples.tr: logD7.4 is about 1.1; nearly neutral in the stomach.
Ionized salicylate is trapped in urine and excreted faster.

advancedTest.explain: Less ionization at 7.4 raises the neutral fraction; logP may barely change.

lessons.title: Measuring & calculating lipophilicity

levels.kid:
How do chemists find out how greasy a medicine is? They have two ways.

**Way 1: test it for real.** Put the medicine in a little tube with water and an oily liquid, shake it like a snow globe, wait, and then measure how much went into each layer.

**Way 2: guess with a computer.** The computer looks at the pieces of the molecule. Each piece has a greasy score, like points in a game. Add up the points and you get a guess.

The computer is super fast, so chemists use it to sort thousands of ideas. But computers can be wrong, so for the best molecules they still do the real shaking test.
levels.hs:
Chemists both **measure** and **calculate** lipophilicity.

**Measuring it**
- **Shake-flask:** the classic "gold standard." Shake the compound in octanol and buffer, let the layers separate, then measure the concentration in each, usually by HPLC. It is accurate but slow, and it struggles with very greasy compounds because almost nothing stays in the water.
- **Chromatography (HPLC):** greasier compounds stick longer to a nonpolar column. Retention time is converted into a lipophilicity value using standards. It is fast, needs very little compound and works well for comparing many molecules.
- **Potentiometric titration:** titrating an ionizable compound with and without octanol shifts its apparent pKa, and the shift gives logP.

**Calculating it** (written cLogP or ClogP)
- **Fragment methods** split the molecule into pieces with known contributions and add them, plus correction factors.
- **Atom-based methods** give every atom type a contribution (the Crippen method is a famous example and is built into common free software).
- **Machine-learning models** learn from large sets of measured data.

Calculated values are usually within about half a log unit for ordinary drug-like molecules but can be off by much more for unusual structures. Teams calculate everything, then measure the compounds that matter.
levels.college:
**Shake-flask (OECD 107).** Octanol and aqueous buffer are mutually pre-saturated; the compound is equilibrated, phases are separated (centrifugation helps break emulsions) and both are quantified. Reliable range is roughly logD -2 to 4. Miniaturized 96-well versions with LC-MS quantification are standard in industry. For very lipophilic compounds the slow-stirring method (OECD 123) avoids micro-emulsions that make the aqueous phase look falsely concentrated.

**Potentiometric (pH-metric).** For ionizable compounds, titration in a two-phase system gives an apparent pKa shifted by partitioning; the shift yields logP of the neutral and, sometimes, of the ion pair. It needs a pKa in a measurable range and adequate solubility.

**Chromatographic.** Reversed-phase retention correlates with lipophilicity. Fast-gradient methods give a Chromatographic Hydrophobicity Index (CHI), which can be scaled to a logD-like value (ChromLogD). Chromatographic values are not on the same absolute scale as octanol: they reward aromaticity and are influenced by the stationary phase's lack of hydrogen-bond basicity, so ChromLogD is often numerically higher than shake-flask logD. Use it for ranking within a series.

**Calculation methods.**
- Fragment-based: Rekker's method, and the Leo/Hansch ClogP with correction factors for proximity, branching and electronic effects.
- Atom-based: Ghose-Crippen and Wildman-Crippen (1999) atom contributions; XLOGP3 adds correction terms.
- Property or ML-based: models trained on large proprietary measured datasets, often retrained per company.

**Accuracy.** Typical errors are about 0.4 to 0.7 log units for drug-like sets, larger for zwitterions, macrocycles, compounds with intramolecular hydrogen bonds and novel heterocycles. Calculated logD requires calculated pKa, and pKa errors add directly.
levels.phd:
**Error structure.** Calculated logP errors are not random noise; they are systematic and chemotype-specific. A model can rank-order a congeneric series well (because shared errors cancel) while being absolutely wrong by a log unit. This is why many groups train local models on their own series' measurements, and why in-house ML models built on tens of thousands of measured logD values usually outperform public equations on in-house chemistry.

**What each assay really measures.**
- Shake-flask measures a thermodynamic equilibrium, but is vulnerable to impurities (a lipophilic impurity at a low level can dominate the octanol phase when detection is not selective), aggregation, adsorption to plastic and incomplete phase separation.
- Chromatographic indices measure a kinetic retention process on an alkyl-bonded silica phase. The stationary phase lacks hydrogen-bond basicity, so the solvation-equation coefficients differ from octanol's. Converting to an octanol scale assumes a constant relationship that breaks down across chemotypes, so ChromLogD and shake-flask logD should not be mixed in one model without calibration.
- Immobilized artificial membrane (IAM) chromatography uses phosphatidylcholine-like stationary phases and captures electrostatic interactions of charged amphiphiles with headgroups, often correlating better with membrane and tissue binding than octanol.

**Computational frontier.** Physics-based approaches compute transfer free energies by alchemical simulations or implicit-solvent models; they handle novel chemotypes in principle but are sensitive to force-field polarization and conformational sampling, especially for flexible, chameleonic molecules whose conformations differ between water and octanol. Graph neural networks and multitask models trained on lipophilicity, solubility and permeability jointly tend to improve each endpoint.

**Reporting standards.** A useful value states method, pH, buffer, ionic strength, temperature and whether it is logP or logD. Many literature disputes about lipophilicity trends turn out to be mixtures of methods.
levels.expert:
Senior medicinal chemists treat lipophilicity data like any other assay: with a known error bar and known failure modes.

**Working habits.**
- Calculate for design, measure for decisions. Anything going into an in vivo study should have measured logD7.4.
- Pick one measurement method per project and stick to it. Changing from shake-flask to chromatographic logD mid-programme produces artificial jumps of a log unit.
- Check calculated values against measured data for your series in the first weeks. If the program is off by a constant amount, correct for it; if it misranks, stop trusting it for that chemotype.
- Flag compounds outside the reliable range. A shake-flask logD of 4.5 may be a floor, not a value.

**Red flags in data.**
- A polar analogue that measures greasier than expected: check purity, aggregation and whether an intramolecular hydrogen bond formed.
- Poor mass balance in shake-flask (compound missing from both phases): adsorption, precipitation or instability.
- A big gap between logD and a cell permeability result: think efflux, pKa error or chameleonic folding.

**Why it matters to patients.** Lipophilicity predictions drive which compounds get made and which reach animals. A programme that systematically underestimates lipophilicity can carry greasy, promiscuous compounds into toxicology studies, where they fail late and expensively. For CNS drugs the margins are tight: a one-unit error in logD can be the difference between a brain-penetrant candidate and one that cannot reach its target.

The best chemists know the approximate cLogP of their key compounds by heart and can estimate a new analogue's value from π constants within seconds, then check it with software.

keyPoints: Shake-flask octanol/buffer is the classic gold-standard measurement.
HPLC retention gives fast, low-material lipophilicity estimates best used for ranking.
cLogP methods: fragment-based, atom-based (Crippen) and machine-learning.
Calculated values are often off by about 0.5 log units, more for unusual scaffolds.
State method and pH; never mix measurement methods in one trend.

examples.tr: Gives measured logD7.4; reliable roughly from -2 to 4.
Fast chromatographic index; often numerically higher than shake-flask logD.
Atom-contribution method implemented in common open-source cheminformatics tools.

lessons.title: Lipophilic efficiency (LipE)

levels.kid:
Imagine two kids win the same race. One trained hard and ran fast. The other wore super-sticky rocket shoes that make a mess everywhere.

Both won, but one won the **good way**.

Medicines are like that. A medicine can stick to its target because it fits really well, like a key in a lock. Or it can stick just because it is **greasy**, and greasy things stick to everything, including the wrong places.

Chemists use a score called **LipE** to tell the difference. It asks: how strong is the medicine, minus how greasy it is? A high LipE means the medicine wins the race the good way, by fitting, not by being sticky.
levels.hs:
**Potency** is how little drug you need to hit the target. Chemists often write it as **pIC50** (or pKi): the negative log of the concentration that gives half the effect. Higher pIC50 = more potent. A pIC50 of 8 means 10 nM; 9 means 1 nM.

The trap: adding greasy groups almost always boosts potency, because greasy molecules are pushed out of water and onto proteins. But greasy compounds also dissolve poorly, get metabolized fast and hit lots of wrong targets.

**Lipophilic efficiency** (LipE, also called LLE) separates good potency from greasy potency:

**LipE = pIC50 - logP** (or logD)

Examples:
- pIC50 8, logP 2 → LipE 6 (excellent)
- pIC50 9, logP 5 → LipE 4 (more potent, but bought with grease)

Many teams aim for a LipE of about 5 or higher for a drug candidate.

How to raise LipE:
- Add groups that make real, specific contacts, such as a hydrogen bond to the target.
- Remove grease that does not help binding.
- Swap a phenyl ring for a pyridine if potency holds, since the nitrogen lowers logP.

If a change raises potency AND logP by the same amount, LipE stays the same: you have not really improved the molecule.
levels.college:
**Definition.** LipE (Leeson and Springthorpe, 2007) = pActivity - logP or logD. Because both are logs, it can be read as the log of potency relative to lipophilicity, roughly how much of the binding free energy is not simply attributable to bulk hydrophobic partitioning.

**Related metrics.**
- **Ligand efficiency (LE)** = 1.37 × pIC50 / heavy atom count (kcal/mol per heavy atom at about 300 K). It normalizes for size; about 0.3 or more is a common target for leads.
- **LELP** = logP / LE (Keserű and Makara), combining size and lipophilicity; lower is better.
- **LLE(AT)** (Mortenson and Murray) adjusts LipE for size to make fragment and lead comparisons fairer.

**Using LipE in practice.**
- Plot pIC50 vs logD for a series. Diagonal lines are constant LipE. Compounds moving up and to the left are improving; moving up and to the right is "potency by grease".
- Matched molecular pairs show which changes add LipE (a new hydrogen bond, a polar atom in a solvent-exposed region) and which only add logP (an extra chlorine in a non-specific pocket).
- Track LipE from hit to candidate. Successful programmes typically increase potency while holding or reducing logD.

**Why it predicts quality.** Analyses of large compound sets associate lower lipophilicity at a given potency with better solubility, lower metabolic clearance, fewer off-target hits and lower toxicity risk. LipE is therefore a proxy for the "quality" of potency.

**Limits.** The metric inherits logP/logD measurement errors, depends on which lipophilicity value is used, ignores efflux and solubility directly, and can be gamed by polar groups that reduce logD but hurt permeability.
levels.phd:
**Thermodynamic reading.** pKd relates to ΔG(binding) = -2.303RT·pKd; logP relates to ΔG(water→octanol). LipE therefore approximates the free energy of transfer from octanol to the binding site: how much better the target's pocket is than a generic lipophilic phase. A LipE of zero means the target is no better than octanol; every unit above that is specific recognition.

**Why hydrophobic potency is "cheap".** Burying nonpolar surface releases ordered water and yields roughly constant free energy per square angstrom regardless of geometric precision. Polar interactions pay a desolvation penalty first; a hydrogen bond only contributes net affinity when the geometry is near-optimal. This asymmetry means random optimization drifts toward lipophilicity, a phenomenon described as **molecular obesity** (Hann, 2011) and documented as property inflation in patent and literature compounds over decades.

**Enthalpy-entropy arguments.** Some groups proposed that enthalpy-driven binders are higher quality, but measured ΔH and -TΔS are heavily influenced by entropy-enthalpy compensation, protonation changes and buffer effects; LipE is a more robust, cheaper metric than calorimetric profiles for driving design.

**Target dependence.** Achievable LipE depends on the binding site. Deep, polar, well-defined pockets (many proteases, kinase hinge regions) allow high LipE. Shallow, lipophilic sites (some protein-protein interfaces, lipid-processing enzymes, nuclear receptors) cap it; there, the benchmark is the best known ligand for that target, not a universal threshold.

**Statistics caveat.** LipE combines two measured quantities with independent errors. Small LipE differences (under about 0.5) between analogues are often within noise. Look for trends across matched pairs rather than single values.
levels.expert:
**How it shows up in project meetings.**
- Every slide with potency also shows LipE or a potency-versus-logD plot. If potency rises by a log unit but logD rose by a log unit too, the honest summary is "no progress".
- Prioritize vectors where small polar additions (an amide NH that hydrogen-bonds a backbone carbonyl, a nitrogen in a ring that faces water) raise LipE. These are the changes that pay off in solubility, clearance and safety later.
- Use LipE together with LE: a fragment hit may have low potency but excellent efficiency; a high-throughput hit may be potent but already greasy and large, with little room to grow.

**Typical milestones (heuristics, not laws).**
- Hit: whatever you have; just measure it.
- Lead: LipE trending up, often around 4 to 5.
- Candidate: often 5 to 7, with the best compounds higher where the pocket allows.

**Pitfalls.**
- Using cLogP for one compound and measured logD for another in the same comparison.
- Chasing LipE with an acid that lowers logD7.4 but kills permeability or brain penetration.
- Ignoring that cellular potency includes permeability and efflux; LipE from cell assays mixes several properties.

**Clinical relevance.** Drugs from high-LipE series tend to need lower exposures for effect and carry fewer off-target liabilities, which matters for patients on many drugs at once, such as ICU and neurosurgical patients who may receive antiseizure drugs, sedatives, antibiotics and anticoagulant reversal agents together. Cleaner molecules mean fewer interactions and side effects. Many of the most successful modern kinase inhibitors and CNS drugs were optimized explicitly with LipE plots on the wall.

keyPoints: LipE (LLE) = pIC50 (or pKi) - logP (or logD).
Grease buys potency cheaply but brings poor solubility, clearance and off-target risk.
Common candidate goal: LipE about 5 or higher.
Constant LipE when potency and logP rise together = no real progress.
Ligand efficiency (LE) normalizes potency by heavy atom count; about 0.3 is a common lead target.

lessons.title: Too greasy: promiscuity & toxicity

levels.kid:
Have you ever touched sticky tape? It sticks to your finger, the table, your hair, everything!

Very greasy medicines are a bit like sticky tape. Instead of sticking only to the one thing they are meant to fix, they stick to lots of other things in your body too.

When a medicine sticks to the wrong things, it can cause problems, like a tummy ache, a funny heartbeat or a tired liver.

Greasy medicines also do not mix well with water, so they are hard to swallow as a pill and hard for blood to carry.

So chemists try hard to keep medicines from being too greasy. Just a little greasy is the sweet spot.
levels.hs:
When logP (or logD) gets high, many things go wrong at once. This is sometimes called the **lipophilicity penalty**.

**1. Promiscuity.** Greasy molecules bind to many proteins they were not designed for, because hydrophobic sticking does not need a precise fit. More off-target binding means more side effects.

**2. Heart risk (hERG).** The hERG potassium channel in the heart has a greasy cavity that traps many lipophilic drugs, especially greasy amines. Blocking it can cause a dangerous heart rhythm. Many drugs have been withdrawn or restricted for this.

**3. Metabolism.** Liver enzymes (cytochrome P450s) prefer greasy molecules, so greasy drugs often get broken down fast and can form reactive metabolites.

**4. Poor solubility.** Greasy compounds dissolve badly, making absorption unpredictable.

**5. Tissue build-up.** Greasy, basic drugs can pile up in tissues and in cell compartments, sometimes causing a condition called phospholipidosis.

A famous analysis from Pfizer found that compounds with high cLogP (above 3) and low polar surface area (below 75 Å²) were much more likely to cause toxicity in animal studies than polar, less greasy compounds. This is the **"3/75 rule"**.

Lesson: keep lipophilicity as low as potency allows.
levels.college:
**Promiscuity.** Large analyses of in vitro panel data show off-target hit rates climbing with logP, and bases are more promiscuous than acids or neutrals at the same lipophilicity, likely because many aminergic GPCRs, transporters and ion channels have anionic, lipophilic sites. Promiscuity predicts in vivo toxicity findings.

**The 3/75 rule.** Hughes and colleagues (Pfizer, 2008) analysed in vivo toxicology outcomes and found that compounds with cLogP > 3 and TPSA < 75 Å² had markedly higher odds of adverse findings than those with cLogP < 3 and TPSA > 75 Å². It is a statistical association, not a hard limit.

**hERG.** The Kv11.1 channel's inner cavity is large and lined with aromatic residues (Tyr652, Phe656), which interact with lipophilic cations via π-stacking and cation-π contacts. Blockade prolongs the QT interval and can precipitate torsades de pointes. Mitigation: lower logD, reduce or remove basicity, add an acid (zwitterion), reduce aromatic ring count, or introduce polarity near the basic centre. Terfenadine was replaced by its zwitterionic metabolite, fexofenadine, which lacks the cardiac liability.

**Metabolic and reactive liabilities.** CYP3A4 and other P450s bind lipophilic substrates; high logD correlates with high intrinsic clearance. Higher turnover gives more chances to form reactive intermediates (epoxides, quinone-imines) that can bind proteins and contribute to idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury. Analyses of DILI have linked risk to the combination of high daily dose and high lipophilicity.

**Phospholipidosis.** Cationic amphiphilic drugs (lipophilic, basic) accumulate in lysosomes, complex with phospholipids and inhibit phospholipases, producing lamellar inclusions seen on electron microscopy. Amiodarone is the classic example.

**Formulation and assay artefacts.** Very lipophilic compounds form colloidal aggregates that inhibit enzymes non-specifically in screens, giving false positives that disappear when detergent is added.
levels.phd:
**Mechanistic basis of promiscuity.** Binding free energy contains a lipophilic component that is relatively insensitive to shape complementarity. As logP rises, this nonspecific contribution can push a compound over the activity threshold at many sites; at low logP, only good shape and polar complementarity yield measurable binding. Statistical analyses (for example, of large selectivity panels) show off-target hit rates rising steeply with lipophilicity, with ionization state modulating the curve: basic compounds hit aminergic targets, acids preferentially hit sites such as albumin and some nuclear receptors.

**hERG structural biology.** Cryo-EM structures of hERG show an unusually large central cavity and hydrophobic pockets extending from it, explaining its unusual drug sensitivity compared with other Kv channels. Ligand pharmacophores emphasize a basic nitrogen flanked by aromatic or lipophilic groups at a distance. Because block is state-dependent and kinetically complex, in vitro IC50 values must be interpreted together with free plasma concentration; the CiPA initiative shifted assessment from hERG IC50 alone to integrated multi-channel and in silico models of proarrhythmia.

**Membrane toxicity.** Highly lipophilic compounds accumulate in membranes and can disrupt mitochondrial function (uncoupling, electron-transport inhibition) and bile acid transport (BSEP inhibition), both implicated in hepatotoxicity. BSEP inhibition and mitochondrial liability are increasingly screened in parallel.

**Property inflation.** Over decades, the average lipophilicity and size of compounds in medicinal chemistry papers and patents rose, even as approved oral drugs remained comparatively constrained. Leeson and Springthorpe argued this drift, driven by potency-centric optimization and target classes with lipophilic sites, contributes to attrition.

**Caveats.** Many successful drugs are lipophilic (some antifungals, kinase inhibitors, lipid-lowering agents); the rule is probabilistic. The real question is whether the lipophilicity is necessary for target engagement and how safety margins compare at the efficacious unbound exposure.
levels.expert:
**How a senior team guards against grease.**
- Set lipophilicity guardrails early (for example, keep logD7.4 below about 3 unless the target clearly demands more), and justify every exception.
- Run a broad off-target panel and hERG on leads, not just candidates. A greasy base with weak hERG binding at the start will usually worsen as potency is optimized.
- Pair cLogP with TPSA, aromatic ring count and fraction of sp3 carbons. Flat, aromatic, greasy molecules carry the most risk.
- Remember the dose: the same intrinsic liability matters more when a drug needs high exposure. Low lipophilicity plus high potency together give the best margins.

**Fixes that work.**
- Replace aromatic rings with saturated or heteroaromatic ones.
- Introduce polarity at solvent-exposed vectors.
- Lower basic pKa or remove the basic centre.
- Add an acid to create a zwitterion where target and distribution allow (the fexofenadine strategy).

**Clinical consequences you will meet as a doctor.**
- QT-prolonging drugs: many lipophilic bases (some antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, antiemetics, macrolide antibiotics) carry QT warnings. In neuro-ICU patients, combining several QT-prolonging drugs with low potassium or magnesium raises the risk of torsades de pointes, so ECG and electrolyte monitoring matter.
- Amiodarone, a very lipophilic cationic amphiphile, causes phospholipidosis-related lung, liver and thyroid toxicity and lingers in tissues for weeks to months.
- Idiosyncratic liver injury, more common with high-exposure lipophilic drugs, is a leading reason for post-marketing warnings and withdrawals.

The practical motto: **potency is easy to buy with grease, but patients pay for it later.**

keyPoints: High lipophilicity raises off-target binding (promiscuity) and toxicity risk.
Pfizer 3/75 rule: cLogP > 3 with TPSA < 75 Å² linked to more in vivo toxicity.
Lipophilic bases tend to block the cardiac hERG channel (QT prolongation).
Greasy drugs tend to show faster CYP metabolism, poorer solubility and tissue build-up.
Fixes: lower logD, add polarity, reduce basicity or aromatic rings.

examples.tr: The zwitterionic metabolite kept antihistamine activity without the cardiac (hERG) liability.
Very lipophilic cationic amphiphile; causes phospholipidosis and lingers in tissues.
Greasy screening hits that inhibit non-specifically; activity vanishes with detergent.
